items.title: Linus Torvalds Reveals Claude Code Wrote Linux Kernel Patches and Test Programs
items.summary: Linus Torvalds has disclosed that Claude Code helped write Linux kernel patches, test programs, review material, and the first draft of a technical write-up under his direction. The work targets page-cache read performance, showing how AI coding tools are used in core operating-system development while openly documenting technical limits. Torvalds states that Claude Code produced the material under his guidance. He separately notes that measurements ran on his machine. The disclosure describes a supervised development effort, not an AI system independently maintaining Linux. The eight-patch series addresses a bottleneck when many threads perform small reads from the same cached file. Each read normally updates a folio reference count. A folio represents a group of memory pages, and repeated updates force processor cores to compete over shared data. The proposed approach delays reusing removed page-cache memory until an RCU grace period ends. This gives active readers time to finish before another purpose can use that memory. With that protection, the new read path can copy cached data without taking and dropping folio references. When conditions prevent the faster route, including missing cached data or a user-buffer fault, the existing read path continues the operation. Linus Torvalds Reveals Claude Code Wrote Linux Patches In the October 10 commit message, Torvalds reported that eight threads on his four-core, eight-thread Intel laptop achieved roughly 30–33 million 16-byte reads per second from a cached file, compared with 9.9–10.4 million in the baseline. Those results apply to a narrow benchmark, not overall Linux performance. Testing used ext4, with processor security mitigations and CONFIG_HARDENED_USERCOPY disabled. We didn’t measure a larger machine, and some reads involving missing user-memory pages became slower. Memory pressure remains a major concern. Delayed frees can leave substantial memory waiting for reuse without the allocator properly accounting for it. Later patches reduced that backlog, but the write-up still lists unresolved allocation problems and no firm bound when grace periods run slowly. One test checked for incorrect data during repeated page eviction and reuse. Normal runs reported no bad reads, while a deliberately broken version returned wrong bytes, including data from other users of freed memory. Testing remained limited. We did not cover KASAN, lockdep, hardened usercopy, other architectures, or several stress cases. The disclosure complements coverage of Claude Code Security and AI-led Linux kernel bug research . AI can support development and investigation, but these patches still need broader testing and review before real workloads can validate their performance gains and memory-safety claims. items.summary_html:
Linus Torvalds has disclosed that Claude Code helped write Linux kernel patches, test programs, review material, and the first draft of a technical write-up under his direction.

The work targets page-cache read performance, showing how AI coding tools are used in core operating-system development while openly documenting technical limits.

Torvalds states that Claude Code produced the material under his guidance. He separately notes that measurements ran on his machine.

The disclosure describes a supervised development effort, not an AI system independently maintaining Linux. The eight-patch series addresses a bottleneck when many threads perform small reads from the same cached file.

Each read normally updates a folio reference count. A folio represents a group of memory pages, and repeated updates force processor cores to compete over shared data.

The proposed approach delays reusing removed page-cache memory until an RCU grace period ends. This gives active readers time to finish before another purpose can use that memory.

With that protection, the new read path can copy cached data without taking and dropping folio references. When conditions prevent the faster route, including missing cached data or a user-buffer fault, the existing read path continues the operation.

Linus Torvalds Reveals Claude Code Wrote Linux Patches

In the October 10 commit message, Torvalds reported that eight threads on his four-core, eight-thread Intel laptop achieved roughly 30–33 million 16-byte reads per second from a cached file, compared with 9.9–10.4 million in the baseline.

Those results apply to a narrow benchmark, not overall Linux performance. Testing used ext4, with processor security mitigations and CONFIG_HARDENED_USERCOPY disabled. We didn’t measure a larger machine, and some reads involving missing user-memory pages became slower.

Memory pressure remains a major concern. Delayed frees can leave substantial memory waiting for reuse without the allocator properly accounting for it. Later patches reduced that backlog, but the write-up still lists unresolved allocation problems and no firm bound when grace periods run slowly.

One test checked for incorrect data during repeated page eviction and reuse. Normal runs reported no bad reads, while a deliberately broken version returned wrong bytes, including data from other users of freed memory.

Testing remained limited. We did not cover KASAN, lockdep, hardened usercopy, other architectures, or several stress cases.

The disclosure complements coverage of Claude Code Security and AI-led Linux kernel bug research. AI can support development and investigation, but these patches still need broader testing and review before real workloads can validate their performance gains and memory-safety claims.

items.title: Critical Adobe Acrobat Flaw Lets Malicious PDFs Trigger One-Click Memory Corruption
items.summary: Adobe has fixed a flaw in Acrobat and Acrobat Reader that lets a malicious PDF corrupt memory when a user opens it. Tracked as CVE-2026-81983, the out-of-bounds write carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and could lead to code execution with the victim’s user rights. Adobe says it has seen no active exploitation so far. The bug sits in Acrobat’s image pipeline, code that starts parsing image data as soon as a PDF opens. Researchers found it with a custom Python fuzzer built largely with help from a large language model. Instead of randomly modifying full PDF files, the tool created small, valid documents. It changed image fields such as width, height, bit depth, color space, filters, and sample bytes. The strongest crash came from a crafted 16-bit image inside a PDF only 745 bytes in size. The root cause is a 32-bit integer overflow in Acrobat.dll. Acrobat calculates the number of image samples by multiplying an image’s width by its color component count. A second size check adds two bytes for every 16-bit sample. With a very large width, this later value wraps to a tiny number, so Acrobat accepts a very short data stream. Adobe Acrobat Flaw The byte-swap loop still sees a huge sample count and keeps reading and writing past the end of a 16-byte buffer. This causes memory corruption and may give an attacker a path to run code. A proof-of-concept image used a width of 536,870,912, a height of one, 16 bits per component, and the DeviceCMYK color space. Four CMYK components produced a sample count of 0x80000000. The size check approves a buffer the loop then overruns (source : remedio ) According to Remedio research , the related byte-size calculation reached 0x100000000 and wrapped to zero in 32-bit math, allowing an eight-byte stream to pass validation. Opening the PDF was enough to reach the faulty image-rendering path. The CVSS vector shows a local attack path, low attack complexity, no privileges, and required user interaction. A successful exploit can have high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. In practice, attackers still need to deliver the malicious document via email, chat, downloads, or another route. Adobe fixed the issue by using 64-bit math to calculate the sample count and rejecting values above INT_MAX before touching memory. The fix arrived in security bulletin APSB26-141 on September 8, 2026. Adobe patched Acrobat and Reader Continuous 26.002.21900 and earlier with version 26.002.21901. Acrobat 2024 Classic 24.001.30383 and earlier was updated to 24.001.30429. Users and administrators should install the fixed releases without delay, keep automatic updates enabled, and treat unexpected PDF attachments with care. Security teams should also filter suspicious PDFs at email gateways and watch for crashes tied to Acrobat.dll. Adobe lists CVE-2026-81983 as critical, while the NVD record confirms that exploitation needs a victim to open a crafted file. The finding also shows how focused, AI-assisted fuzzing can find deep bugs in old file parsers. Readers can review our earlier coverage of Adobe Acrobat Reader flaws that allow arbitrary code execution and the Adobe Acrobat zero-day exploited through malicious PDFs for wider context on PDF security risks. items.title: PoC Exploit Released for Critical GitLab RCE Vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229)
items.summary: A public proof-of-concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-97229 published by researcher Jonah Burgess shows how a flaw in GitLab’s CI/CD regular-expression compiler could be used to run commands on a vulnerable server. GitLab rates the issue Critical with a CVSS score of 10.0. The exploit code is publicly available, raising the risk for organizations that have not yet installed the security updates. The PoC targets GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. Its author reports testing the included exploit layout against the official Linux amd64 GitLab CE 19.4.1 image. The code uses GitLab’s CI lint endpoint, which checks CI/CD configuration files, as part of the exploit chain. The exploit has an important access condition. The attacker needs permission to push a branch to a public project on the affected GitLab instance. The PoC then sends a later request to the CI lint endpoint without a token, cookie, or other authorization header. Jonah Burgess says the command runs as GitLab’s git account, not as an administrator. The public code is an initial release, and its author says further analysis of affected configurations and other possible paths is ongoing. PoC Exploit Released for Critical GitLab Vulnerability GitLab’s advisory describes CVE-2026-97229 as an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler . The PoC details a chain in which CI lint reads a crafted pipeline configuration from an attacker-controlled branch and processes a regular expression against specially named repository paths. A Unicode path causes Ruby to compile the expression again after GitLab’s size check. The exploit authors say this leads to an integer overflow that redirects the regular-expression engine’s execution and reaches a command-execution function. The repository reports that the test request usually ends with an HTTP 502 error because the worker process crashes after the command runs. That response alone does not confirm successful exploitation. Jonah Burgess author’s tests , command output returned through a callback indicated execution. The PoC also requires substantial memory, and the published layout is specific to one GitLab build. The author warns that low memory or multiple concurrent requests could instead disrupt service. GitLab says the flaw affects CE and EE versions 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. The company released those fixed versions on October 12, 2026, and strongly recommends that self-managed installations upgrade promptly. GitLab.com is already running a patched version, while GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. Administrators should confirm their version and upgrade to the fixed release for their branch or a later supported version. They should also review recent changes to CI/CD configuration files, especially new or modified regular expressions and project branches. GitLab’s earlier CI/CD regex security coverage and previous security-update reporting provide additional context on why these pipeline components deserve close review. This PoC does not establish that the vulnerability is being used in real-world intrusions. However, it gives defenders a concrete reason to prioritize patching: the issue has the highest CVSS rating, and public exploit code describes a path from project write access to command execution on a vulnerable server. items.title: Critical Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Attackers Escape Virtual Machines and Take Control of Hosts
items.summary: A critical flaw in the Linux kernel may allow an attacker-controlled virtual machine (VM) to breach its isolation boundary and impact the host system. This vulnerability, identified as CVE-2026-99999 and referred to as PwnEscape by researcher Paulos Yibelo, originates from the Linux networking code rather than a specific hypervisor. Paulos Yibelo demonstrated a technique that exposes host memory and, in their lab, progressed to host-level code execution. The flaw is serious for cloud providers and organizations that run untrusted workloads in virtual machines. VM isolation is meant to stop code inside one guest from reaching the host and other workloads. PwnEscape shows how a weakness in a host’s packet-processing path can threaten that boundary, even when the underlying issue is not in the hypervisor itself. PwnEscape Kernel Vulnerability Linux can delay calculating a network packet’s checksum. This is a normal performance feature: packet metadata tells the kernel where the checksum operation should begin and where the result should be written. According to Paulos Yibelo’s PwnEscape report , the problem occurred when less-trusted packet metadata could influence a later write into an IPv4 header. Linux had already processed the packet using the header’s earlier contents. But before fragmentation, the deferred checksum operation could change those contents. Later code then relied on the updated IPv4 header length. In Paulos Yibelo’s test case, the packet initially appeared to have a standard 20-byte IPv4 header. After the deferred write, the header could be interpreted as 60 bytes long. The fragmentation code could then treat bytes beyond the packet’s valid linear data as part of the header and include them in an outgoing packet. He reported that this exposed 32 bytes of host memory. That disclosure is not the same as code execution. The report describes a separate, controlled lab chain in which researchers used host-memory observations and carefully managed allocation behavior to demonstrate selected kernel-memory writes and run a host-root helper. They say this result was reproduced on researcher-owned systems, not as proof of root execution in a cloud provider’s production environment. The distinction matters for readers assessing the risk. A host-memory leak can reveal information that should remain outside a guest’s reach. Further steps may be needed to turn that primitive into control of the host, and the report does not establish that every Linux VM or hypervisor is equally vulnerable. Linux kernel branch Affected versions within the branch First fixed version 5.10 5.10 through 5.10.271 5.10.272 5.15 5.15 through 5.15.222 5.15.223 6.1 6.1 through 6.1.189 6.1.190 6.6 6.6 through 6.6.158 6.6.159 6.12 6.12 through 6.12.112 6.12.113 6.18 6.18 through 6.18.56 6.18.57 7.2 7.2 through 7.2.10 7.2.11 7.3 development series Release candidates before 7.3-rc7 7.3-rc7 The upstream Linux patch adds a check before certain checksum-completion operations. It verifies that the checksum start is not inside the IPv4 header. If the metadata fails the check, the kernel does not proceed with that checksum write along the affected path. The change covers several consumers, including IPv4 fragmentation. The commit describes the change as a defense-in-depth measure. It also notes that stronger validation at packet input needs more work. In other words, the patch adds protection at places where the kernel completes checksums, but it is not presented as a full redesign of how all checksum metadata enters the networking stack. Administrators should review their Linux vendor’s security notices and install an updated kernel that includes the fix. The upstream commit can help identify the change, but Linux distributions may backport security fixes to older kernel versions. A version number alone may not show whether a system is protected, so check the vendor’s advisory and confirm that the system is running the updated kernel. PwnEscape reminds us that VM security depends on more than the hypervisor. Guest traffic also passes through host operating-system components, including networking code. When metadata can trigger a write later in packet processing, checks made earlier may no longer describe the packet that a later component sees. The discovery emerged from Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge, which invited researchers to test its isolation controls. Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai reported the Linux kernel flaw on the third day while working from a standard sandbox without special access. Vercel called it the program’s most important finding. The challenge received 1,285 reports over two weeks and paid $242,000 in total bounties, with the kernel flaw accounting for its only critical-rated finding. Cybersecurity News has also covered Vercel’s confirmation of a KVM escape report and a separate Linux vhost flaw with a public proof of concept . These are distinct issues with different causes. They should not be treated as interchangeable or assumed to be fixed by the same patch. For defenders, the immediate step is to track vendor updates and patch Linux hosts that run virtual machines. The underlying failure was a mismatch between packet metadata and the IPv4 header that later code trusted. That makes the fix important not only for virtualization providers but also for teams that depend on Linux network processing to keep untrusted workloads contained. An EDR alert reveals an attack.
